source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Curran_2016_KeepOffTheGrass.pdf, pp. 293-306: text pp. 293-303 in full (Boxes 1-4 and figure legends included); reference list pp. 303-306 read for every reference cited in the passages used. Pp. 294, 297-299 and 301-302 checked on rendered pages for paragraph structure and numbers. Narrative review: no search or selection method stated.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim reports Curran's 'converging to show' statement as Curran's, names its two citations and correctly says the receptor finding is not a test of cognition.
claims.note: Curran's two citations for the 4-6 weeks statement are ref 58 (Pope et al., 2001, a single study) and ref 59 (Schreiner & Dunn, 2012, a meta-analysis); 'about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence' is Hirvonen et al. (2012, ref 30): '~4 weeks of continuously monitored abstinence' in a secure research unit, with cortical CB1 receptor density back to control levels. Not in the claim, all pointing the same way: Curran adds that one recent study (D'Souza et al., 2016, ref 31) found receptor recovery after as little as 2 days (p. 298), and says on p. 297, citing a review (Crane et al., 2013), that some studies find deficits in the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of deficits at 28 days. Against this, Box 1 (p. 294) describes the Dunedin decline as still apparent in people using less than once a week at 38, the reading the claim corrects from Meier et al. (2012).

anchors.extracted: Dunedin (cohort of 1,037 born 1972-73; IQ at 7-13 and 38): persistent dependence associated with a decline of up to 6 IQ points, particularly with adolescent onset, and still apparent in people using cannabis less than once a week at 38.

anchors.locator: Cognition, learning and memory > Long-term effects, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Case-control studies of non-acute effects inconsistent, tending to mirror acute findings; most consistent is impaired encoding of new episodic memories, with some studies finding deficits in the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of persisting deficits at 28 days (citing a 2013 review, ref 25).

anchors.locator: Cognition, learning and memory > Effects persisting after stopping use (single paragraph)
anchors.extracted: Several studies said to converge on cognitive impairments not persisting beyond 4-6 weeks of abstinence (two sources cited, refs 58 and 59); PET study (ref 30): cortical CB1 receptor downregulation correlated with years of use and returned to control levels after about 4 weeks of continuously monitored abstinence in a secure research unit, and in one recent study (ref 31) after as little as 2 days; imaging studies of persisting effects are cross-sectional and confounded; longitudinal studies needed for people who start in adolescence.

claims.overstatement: None; Curran is not named in the statement.
claims.note: Curran agrees that long-term memory impairments are reported mainly with frequent, heavy use and that confounding prevents causal conclusions (p. 297; Conclusions p. 302). It differs from Broyd on attention: Curran calls findings for working memory, attention and impulsivity mixed (p. 297), whereas the claim reports Broyd's rating of attention as strong and largely consistent; a clause noting that a narrative review of the same year calls attention findings mixed would show the disagreement.

anchors.locator: Cognition, learning and memory > Long-term effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 296)
anchors.extracted: Studies of long-term effects rely mainly on retrospective self-reported use (p. 296); long-term memory impairments reported mainly in frequent, heavy users, but baseline cognition, alcohol and other drugs, type of cannabis, age at onset, depression and addiction confound cause and effect.

anchors.locator: Cognition, learning and memory > Long-term effects, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Case-control findings inconsistent, mirroring acute effects; most consistent is impaired encoding of new episodic memories, with little evidence of deficits at 28 days; findings for working memory, attention and impulsivity mixed; one study found no decision-making difference against controls matched for mental-health confounds, though poorer accuracy correlated with the number of addiction symptoms.

anchors.locator: Conclusions and future directions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Evidence of clear causality lacking; undesired effects may range from mild cognitive impairment to disabling psychiatric disorders; problems mainly observed in heavy, frequent users; non-problematic levels of use unknown.

claims.overstatement: None. One description differs from Curran's text: Curran describes the 3-year study's sample as 'daily users' (p. 301), while the claim says 'people who used frequently', which matches the title of Curran's ref 215 (van der Pol et al., 2013, 'transition from frequent cannabis use to cannabis dependence'). Probably right for the primary study, but the claim attributes the description to Curran.
claims.note: Curran's text: variables directly related to cannabis use did not predict transition to 'addiction' (the study's outcome was dependence, by its title); living alone, coping motives and negative life events (such as a major financial crisis) were 'more important'. The same subsection names early adolescent onset and frequent (especially daily) use as risk factors, citing two studies (Coffey et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2005), with concurrent tobacco use (three studies), and gives European treatment data (mean age at first treatment 24, at first use 16; 83% male). Box 3 (p. 299) lists the DSM-IV dependence criteria, including use in larger amounts or over a longer period than intended and a great deal of time spent obtaining, using or recovering, which supports the editors' remark that frequent use is partly built into the criteria.

anchors.extracted: DSM-IV dependence criteria listed include taking cannabis in larger amounts or over a longer period than intended and spending a great deal of time obtaining, using or recovering from it.

Only a minority of people who use cannabis become addicted; concurrent tobacco use (refs 128-130) and early adolescent onset and frequent, especially daily, use (refs 128, 131) named as risk factors; males have earlier opportunity, greater risk and faster progression; European treatment data: mean age at first treatment 24, at first use 16, 83% male. No figures given for frequency or onset.

A 3-year prospective study of 'daily users' (ref 215, van der Pol et al., 2013, titled on frequent cannabis use): variables directly related to cannabis use did not predict transition to addiction; current factors such as living alone, coping motives and negative life events were more important; a meta-analysis of 24 twin studies attributes 55% of vulnerability to addiction to genes, 17.5% to shared and 27.5% to non-shared environment.

claims.note: Curran's 8.9% (cocaine 20.9%, alcohol 22.7%, tobacco 67.5%) is cited to ref 64, Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011, NESARC), as the claim says; Curran calls DSM-IV dependence 'becoming addicted' and gives no interval. Box 3 supports the claim's description of DSM-5 cannabis use disorder (2 or more symptoms within 12 months, mild with 2-3; eleven criteria counting the seven DSM-IV dependence items, three of the four abuse items and craving), which the claim cites to Connor et al. (2021).

anchors.locator: Cannabis addiction > Cannabis addiction and withdrawal, 1st paragraph (continued in the right column)
anchors.extracted: Estimated chance of becoming addicted after lifetime exposure 8.9%, against cocaine 20.9%, alcohol 22.7% and tobacco 67.5%, cited to ref 64 (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, NESARC).
DSM-5 cannabis use disorder: at least 2 symptoms within a 12-month period; mild 2-3, moderate 4-5, severe 6 or more; DSM-IV abuse and dependence combined, legal-problems item dropped, craving added.

claims.overstatement: None; Curran is not named in the statement.
claims.note: Curran gives 'up to 6 IQ points' for persistent dependence (Box 1, p. 294) and 'around 8 IQ points' for dependence that began in adolescence and persisted (p. 298), consistent with the claim (99.68 to 93.93 = 5.75 points in the 38 people; -0.54 SD x 15 = about 8.1 points in the 23 with onset before 18). Curran's 1,037 is the cohort, not the 874 analysed. Two qualifiers the claim does not carry: Box 1 describes a third prospective cohort, the UK birth cohort of 2,235 adolescents aged 15-16 (Mokrysz et al., 2016, a study by one of Curran's co-authors), in which cumulative use was not associated with lower IQ after pre-teen IQ and confounders (notably tobacco and alcohol use) were taken into account, with only 72 reporting more than 50 uses; and Curran says the Dunedin cohort's older, lower-potency cannabis limits its relevance today (p. 294). Box 1's statement that all studies ignored residual effects on IQ testing is not accurate for Dunedin, which, as the claim says, left out recent use in a sensitivity analysis.

anchors.locator: Box 1, 'Does cannabis affect IQ?', 1st to 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Three large prospective cohorts: Dunedin (1,037; IQ at 7-13 and 38) decline of up to 6 IQ points with persistent dependence, especially with adolescent onset, still apparent with less than weekly use at 38; UK birth cohort (2,235 aged 15-16) no association after pre-teen IQ and confounders, only 72 with more than 50 uses; US twin cohort (3,066 aged 17-20) no IQ difference in twin pairs discordant for use, only 47 pairs with frequent use (more than 30 uses and/or daily); authors read the UK and US results as pointing to genetic or environmental factors, noting younger participants with fewer exposures; all studies used retrospective self-report.

anchors.locator: Cognition, learning and memory > Age-dependent effects: adolescence and adulthood, 7th paragraph (begins 'In terms of neurocognitive function')
anchors.extracted: Dunedin: addiction that began in adolescence and persisted into adulthood associated with a decline of around 8 IQ points; two recent large studies said to cast doubt on a causal explanation.

claims.overstatement: Mild. 'THC relieves the symptoms in a dose-dependent way' generalizes Curran's 'can be alleviated by THC in a dose-dependent manner', which rests on one laboratory study of oral THC (ref 73, Budney et al., 2007, by its title). As worded it can read as a suggestion to use more cannabis to ease withdrawal; naming the study condition (oral THC under laboratory conditions) and Curran's note that dronabinol and nabiximols eased withdrawal without reducing use (p. 301) would avoid that.
claims.note: All other Curran attributions recovered on p. 299: around 50% of daily users on stopping, cited to an earlier review (ref 71, Budney et al., 2004); onset 1-2 days, peak 2-6 days, remission 1-2 weeks (the 'one account'); prominent symptoms craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea (ref 72, Allsop et al., 2011); combined cannabis and tobacco withdrawal stronger than either alone in people who use both daily (ref 77, Vandrey et al., 2008, a within-person comparison). Curran also links symptoms to lower CB1 receptor availability in early abstinence.

anchors.locator: Cannabis addiction > Cannabis addiction and withdrawal, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Withdrawal syndrome affects around 50% of daily users on stopping (citing a 2004 review, ref 71); begins 1-2 days after stopping, peaks at 2-6 days, remits at 1-2 weeks; prominent symptoms craving, sleep problems, nightmares, anger, irritability, dysphoria and nausea; symptoms correlate with reduced CB1 receptor availability; can be alleviated by THC dose-dependently (one oral-THC study, ref 73); in daily users of cannabis and tobacco, combined withdrawal stronger than either alone (ref 77).

anchors.locator: Cannabis addiction > Possible treatments for cannabis addiction, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Dronabinol (oral synthetic THC) and nabiximols attenuated withdrawal symptoms and improved retention but did not reduce cannabis use against placebo; no pharmacotherapy approved.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high (search and selection high; the other four domains some concerns). The count of at least 19 references with a review author matches a rough recount (19 found among 205 parsed entries).

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it substantial rather than minor. The abstract is restrained, but the body states recovery within 4-6 weeks as a convergence of evidence on two sources with receptor normalisation as further support, turns a first-episode psychosis case-control estimate into a fivefold chance of schizophrenia, and gives an uncomputed ninefold estimate; these are the statements the encyclopedia's claims draw on (the after-stopping claim cites the 4-6 weeks statement). A judgment call; the card's own list of gaps supports either rating.

missed: Box 1 (p. 294) says all IQ studies 'ignored possible residual effects of the drug on IQ test performance'. For Dunedin this is not so: Broyd et al. (2016, AM p. 9) describe Meier et al. (2012) as ruling out recent cannabis use, and the teen-IQ claim reports the sensitivity analysis leaving out use in the day or week before testing. Worth a reporting issue; the review's measurement critique should not be carried into claims for Dunedin.
Box 1 gives Dunedin as '1,037 38-year-old individuals'; that is the cohort, not the number analysed (874 per the teen-IQ claim). Minor.

Box 1 reports only the within-pair result of the US twin study (no difference between discordant twins); the between-family comparison is not mentioned, so the box cannot be cited for the US study's overall finding.
